paragraphs.text: Ancient People in the Sahara On 13 October 2000, a small team of palaeontologists led by Paul Sereno of the University of Chicago clambered out of three battered Land Rovers, filled their water bottles and scattered on foot across the toffee-coloured sands of the Ténéré Desert in northern Niger. The Ténéré, one of the most barren areas on Earth, is located on the southern flank of the Sahara. According to the turbaned Tuareg nomads, who have ruled this infertile domain for a few centuries, this California-sized ocean of sand and rock is a ‘desert within a desert’. In the Ténéré Desert, massive dunes might stretch a hundred miles, as far as the eye can see. In addition, 120-degree heat waves and inexorable winds can drain almost all the water from a human body in less than a day.

Mike Hettwer, the team’s photographer, was attracted by the scenery and walked to several dunes to take photos of the landscape. On reaching the first dune, he was shocked to find that the dunes were strewn with many bones. He photographed these bones with his digital camera and hurried back to the Land Rover. ‘I found some bones,’ Hettwer told the other team members. ‘To my great surprise, they don’t belong to dinosaurs. They are human bones.’

One day in the spring of 2005, Paul Sereno contacted Elena Garcea, a prestigious archaeologist at the University of Cassino in Italy, asking her to return to the site with him. After spending 30 years researching the history of the Nile in Sudan and of the mountains in the Libyan Desert, Garcea had become well acquainted with the lives of ancient people in the Sahara. She had not known Sereno before this expedition. His claim to have found so many skeletons in the Ténéré seemed implausible to some archaeologists, one of whom dismissed him as a ‘moonlighting palaeontologist’. However, Garcea was fascinated by the prospect and accepted his invitation.

Over the following three weeks, Sereno and Garcea (along with five excavators, five Tuareg guides, and five soldiers from Niger’s army) made a detailed map of the site, which was dubbed Gobero after the Tuareg name for the area, where the ancient Kiffian and Tenerian nomads used to roam. After that, they excavated eight tombs and found twenty artefacts belonging to the two cultures. From these artefacts, it was evident that Kiffian fishermen caught not only small fish but also some huge ones: the remains of Nile perch, a fierce fish weighing about 300 pounds, along with those of crocodiles and hippos, were left in the vicinity of dunes.

Sereno returned with selected bones and artefacts and began planning the next trip to the Sahara. Meanwhile, he carefully extracted teeth from the skeletons and sent them to a research laboratory for radiocarbon dating. The results indicated that the smaller ‘sleeping’ burials dated to about 6,000 years ago, well within the Tenerian period, whereas the larger, tightly bound burials were approximately 9,000 years old, from the height of the Kiffian period. The scientists could now distinguish one culture from the other.

In the autumn of 2006, the team returned to Gobero with additional crew members and six specialists to exhume another 80 burials. At the site, Chris Stojanowski, a bioarchaeologist at Arizona State University, pieced together further clues. Judging from the bones, the Kiffians appeared peaceful and hardworking. ‘The absence of injuries to their heads or forearms suggests that they did not fight much,’ he said. ‘They were also strongly built.’ Pointing to a long, narrow femur, he explained that its muscle attachment indicated huge leg muscles, a strenuous lifestyle and a protein-rich diet—all consistent with people who lived by fishing. In contrast, the same ridge was barely visible on the femur of a Tenerian male. ‘This individual had a less strenuous lifestyle, which you might expect of a herder.’

Stojanowski concluded that the Tenerians were herders, consistent with the prevailing view of life in the Sahara 6,000 years ago, when the drying climate favoured herding over hunting. But Sereno raised a puzzling question: if the Tenerians were herders, where were their herds? Among thousands of animal bones excavated at Gobero, the team found only three cow skeletons and no remains of goats or sheep. Elena Garcea noted that herding people do not commonly kill their cattle, particularly in a cemetery, and that even modern pastoralists such as Niger’s Wodaabe are reluctant to slaughter animals from their herds. Sereno suggested that the Tenerians at Gobero may have been a transitional group that still relied heavily on hunting and fishing and had not fully adopted herding.
